h1: How Should a Sling Fit After Shoulder Surgery?
keywords: how should a sling fit after shoulder surgery
answer: An arm sling should hold your elbow snugly in the back corner of the pouch, support your forearm and wrist so your hand sits level with or slightly above the elbow, keep your shoulder relaxed rather than hunched, and spread the strap's weight across your neck and opposite shoulder. After surgery, your surgeon's positioning instructions come first.
intro: Slings range from a simple triangular bandage to a padded shoulder immobilizer with a waist strap and a small pillow that holds the arm slightly away from the body. After shoulder surgery you'll usually be given a specific sling and shown how to wear it, often including when it can come off. This page covers what a good fit looks like in general, so you can spot when something has slipped or needs adjusting. It doesn't replace your care team's instructions.

checklist.good: The elbow sits all the way into the back corner of the pouch, so the pouch cups it and the arm can't slide backward.
checklist.tooTight: The pouch is too small or short, so the elbow is pushed forward out of the corner.
checklist.tooLoose: The elbow floats in a baggy pouch or slides out the back.

checklist.good: The forearm is supported along its length, with the hand level with or slightly above the elbow, roughly across the lower chest or upper abdomen. Follow your surgeon's direction if they gave a different angle.
checklist.tooTight: The strap is so short that the hand is hiked up toward the chin and the shoulder is pushed up.
checklist.tooLoose: The strap is so long that the hand and wrist drop below the elbow and the arm hangs.

checklist.good: The pouch reaches to the wrist or the base of the fingers, so the wrist stays straight and supported, with the fingers free to see and move.
checklist.tooTight: Too short: the pouch stops partway up the forearm and the wrist bends down over the edge.
checklist.tooLoose: Too long: the pouch covers the fingers or extends past the hand, so you can't check them or the pouch bunches.

checklist.good: Both shoulders sit level and relaxed, with the injured shoulder neither hunched up nor dragged down.
checklist.tooTight: The injured shoulder is hitched up toward the ear because the strap is too short.
checklist.tooLoose: The shoulder droops forward or down because the arm's weight isn't supported.

checklist.good: The strap crosses the back of the neck to the opposite shoulder, lies flat, and the padding sits where the strap would otherwise rub.
checklist.tooTight: The strap digs into the side of the neck, leaves a red mark or makes you tilt your head.
checklist.tooLoose: The strap slides off the shoulder or the buckle rests on the collarbone.

checklist.good: The waist strap holds the arm and any pillow steady against the body, with room to slide two fingers underneath.
checklist.tooTight: The strap presses into the stomach or makes breathing or sitting uncomfortable.
checklist.tooLoose: The pillow or arm shifts when you walk, or the arm can swing away from the body.

variations.heading: Types of slings and how each should sit
variations.intro: The basic checkpoints are the same: elbow back, forearm supported, wrist straight, shoulder relaxed. Each type gets there a little differently.

items.name: Pouch sling
items.text: A fabric pouch with one adjustable strap. It's the most common type for minor injuries. Fit is mostly about pouch length and strap length: elbow in the back corner, wrist supported at the front, hand at or just above elbow height.

items.name: Shoulder immobilizer
items.text: A pouch sling plus a waist strap that holds the upper arm against the body. The waist strap is what stops the shoulder moving, so it should be snug enough to hold the arm steady without pressing into the stomach.

items.name: Abduction sling with pillow
items.text: Often used after shoulder surgery. A small pillow at the waist holds the arm slightly out from the body. The pillow should sit at the side of the waist, not in front of the stomach, and the arm should rest on it without being pushed forward or backward. Your care team will show you the intended position.

items.name: Triangular bandage
items.text: A large fabric triangle often used in first aid. The same rules apply: support the forearm and wrist, keep the hand at or slightly above the elbow, and tie the knot to the side of the neck rather than on the spine, padding it if it rubs.

items.name: Collar and cuff
items.text: A strap that holds the wrist rather than the whole forearm. It's used only for certain injuries where a doctor wants the arm's weight to hang; don't swap to this type unless you've been told to.

measure.heading: How to choose a size and adjust a sling
measure.intro: Most pouch slings are sized by forearm length, though some brands use other measurements. If your sling was supplied after surgery, it has usually been chosen for you; these steps help you check and readjust it.
steps: Bend the elbow to about a right angle and measure from the back of the elbow to the base of the fingers or the wrist, whichever the brand's chart asks for.
Match that length to the brand's size chart. If you're between sizes, follow the brand's guidance or ask your care team.
Slide the arm into the pouch and push the elbow all the way back into the corner.
Bring the strap around the back of the neck to the front of the pouch and adjust it until the hand sits level with or slightly above the elbow.
Check that the wrist is supported at the front edge and the fingers are free.
Add the waist strap or pillow if your sling has one, snug enough to hold the arm steady with room for two fingers underneath.
Look in a mirror: shoulders level, strap flat, padding in place. Readjust if anything has slipped.
measure.tip: Ask someone to help with the first few adjustments, and ask your care team to show you before you leave if you'll be putting it on yourself.

problems.problem: The neck strap rubs or causes a sore spot
problems.fix: Center the padding over the spot where the strap crosses the neck, or add a soft pad or folded cloth under the strap. Check the strap isn't so short that the arm's weight is pulling up on it.

problems.problem: The hand keeps dropping below the elbow
problems.fix: Shorten the strap and push the elbow back into the corner of the pouch. If the wrist still bends over the edge, the pouch may be too short.

problems.problem: The elbow slides out the back
problems.fix: The pouch may be too big, or the elbow isn't seated in the corner. Reposition the arm, and try a smaller size if it keeps happening.

problems.problem: Fingers or hand feel numb, tingly or look swollen or discolored
problems.fix: Loosen any straps that might be too tight and check the arm isn't being squeezed. If the symptoms don't settle quickly, contact your surgeon, doctor or care team.
Re-center it at the side of the waist and tighten the waist strap slightly. Your care team can recheck the position at your follow-up.

extra.heading: Sleeping and dressing with a sling
extra.body: After shoulder surgery many people are told to sleep in the sling, often propped up with pillows or in a recliner. Loose, front-opening shirts are easier to put on, usually with the surgical arm first. Whether and when you can remove the sling to dress, wash or do exercises depends on your surgeon's instructions.

extra.heading: Checks to do each day
extra.body: Look at the skin under the strap and at the elbow and wrist for redness or rubbing, and check that the fingers are a normal color and you can feel and move them as advised. Readjust the sling after you've been lying down or moving around, since straps loosen and pouches shift during the day.

picks.label: Padded pouch arm sling
picks.why: Wider, padded straps spread the arm's weight more comfortably across the neck and shoulder.

picks.label: Shoulder immobilizer with waist strap
picks.why: Holds the upper arm steady against the body, for situations where the care team wants the shoulder kept still.

picks.label: Neck strap pad for slings
picks.why: A soft add-on pad that reduces rubbing where the strap crosses the neck.

faqs.q: How should a sling fit after shoulder surgery?
faqs.a: The elbow should sit in the back corner of the pouch, the forearm and wrist should be supported with the hand at or slightly above the elbow, and any waist strap or pillow should hold the arm steady. Follow your surgeon's specific positioning.

faqs.q: How high should my arm be in a sling?
faqs.a: Generally with the hand level with or slightly above the elbow, so the arm isn't hanging. Your care team may want a different angle depending on the procedure.

faqs.q: How tight should a sling be?
faqs.a: Snug enough that the arm doesn't drop or swing, but not so tight that the strap digs into the neck or the waist strap presses on your stomach. You should be able to slide two fingers under the straps.

faqs.q: Should my fingers stick out of the sling?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Leaving the fingers free lets you check their color and feeling and move them as your care team advises.

faqs.q: Where should the pillow sit on an abduction sling?
faqs.a: At the side of your waist, so the arm rests slightly away from the body. It shouldn't be in front of your stomach or behind your hip.

faqs.q: What if my sling is uncomfortable?
faqs.a: Check the elbow is seated, the strap padding is in place and the strap length puts the hand at elbow height. If it still hurts, or your hand becomes numb or swollen, contact your care team.

caution: This page covers general sling fit only. After surgery or an injury, follow the positioning and wearing instructions from your surgeon, doctor or physical therapist, and contact them if you have numbness, tingling, color changes, increasing swelling or pain.
